items.stem: Which of the following best describes "feedback loop (bias)"?
options: An independent examination of an algorithmic system to check its accuracy, fairness, legality and impacts
A structured evaluation of the potential risks and effects of an algorithmic system before and during its use
When biased outputs influence future data, reinforcing the bias, as in predictive policing
The EU regulation (in force from August 2024) that classifies AI systems by risk – unacceptable, high, limited and minimal – with obligations for each level
items.answer: When biased outputs influence future data, reinforcing the bias, as in predictive policing
items.markingKey: C. "feedback loop (bias)" is when biased outputs influence future data, reinforcing the bias, as in predictive policing.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The Gender Shades study found the lowest error rates for darker-skinned women.
Reason (R): Facial-analysis systems were trained mainly on lighter-skinned male faces.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. Error rates were highest for darker-skinned women; R is true.

items.stem: Explain why under-representation in training data leads to higher error rates for some groups.
items.answer: If a model sees few examples of a group (e.g. darker-skinned faces), it learns their features poorly, so its predictions for that group are less accurate, as Gender Shades showed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If a model sees few examples of a group (e.g. darker-skinned faces), it learns their features poorly, so its predictions for that group are less accurate, as Gender Shades showed. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An audit of a credit-scoring model that flags "high-risk" borrowers looked only at people who repaid their loans in full. Of 400 such women, 146 were wrongly flagged; of 200 such men, 36 were wrongly flagged. Calculate the false positive rate for each group.
items.answer: women: 36.5%; men: 18%

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"If you train a machine on biased data, you get biased results – at scale and with a veneer of objectivity."
— Joy Buolamwini, founder of the Algorithmic Justice League, interview 2019

With reference to the source, explain two reasons why algorithmic bias is a serious concern.
items.answer: It operates at scale, affecting many people at once, and it appears objective ("veneer of objectivity"), so people are less likely to question or challenge it.
items.markingKey: It operates at scale, affecting many people at once, and it appears objective ("veneer of objectivity"), so people are less likely to question or challenge it. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student claims: "Removing race from the input data guarantees that an algorithm is not racially biased." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Proxies such as postcode, income or arrest history correlate with race, so bias can persist; fairness must be tested on outcomes, not assumed from inputs.
items.markingKey: Proxies such as postcode, income or arrest history correlate with race, so bias can persist; fairness must be tested on outcomes, not assumed from inputs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse the sources of bias in one algorithmic system you have studied and evaluate the measures taken to reduce it.
items.answer: E.g. COMPAS, Gender Shades systems, Amazon CV tool, Dutch childcare benefits; sources: data, proxies, design, deployment; measures: retraining with diverse data, audits, regulation (NYC LL144, EU AI Act), abandonment; evaluate effectiveness.
items.markingKey: E.g. COMPAS, Gender Shades systems, Amazon CV tool, Dutch childcare benefits; sources: data, proxies, design, deployment; measures: retraining with diverse data, audits, regulation (NYC LL144, EU AI Act), abandonment; evaluate effectiveness.

items.stem: "Algorithmic bias is mainly a problem of biased data." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Biased data is a major source, but bias also comes from design and deployment; fixing data alone is insufficient.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: under-representation and historical bias in data (Gender Shades, Amazon); better data can reduce error gaps. Arguments against: design choices – goals, proxies, definitions of fairness – also create bias; deployment context (who uses it, how) matters; some fairness criteria cannot all be satisfied at once. Supported judgement: Biased data is a major source, but bias also comes from design and deployment; fixing data alone is insufficient. items.stem: Explain why algorithmic bias can be more harmful than individual human bias.
items.answer: An algorithm applies the same biased rule consistently to thousands or millions of cases, often invisibly and with an appearance of objectivity, making the harm larger and harder to detect and challenge.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An algorithm applies the same biased rule consistently to thousands or millions of cases, often invisibly and with an appearance of objectivity, making the harm larger and harder to detect and challenge. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why an algorithm trained on historical data may discriminate even if it does not use race or gender as inputs.
items.answer: Historical data records past discrimination, and other variables (postcode, school, gaps in employment) act as proxies for protected characteristics, so the model learns and reproduces the same unequal patterns.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Historical data records past discrimination, and other variables (postcode, school, gaps in employment) act as proxies for protected characteristics, so the model learns and reproduces the same unequal patterns. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between indirect (proxy) discrimination and direct discrimination.
items.answer: Direct discrimination uses a protected characteristic (e.g. gender) as an input; indirect discrimination arises when neutral-seeming variables (e.g. postcode) correlate with it and produce unequal outcomes.
items.markingKey: Direct discrimination uses a protected characteristic (e.g. gender) as an input; indirect discrimination arises when neutral-seeming variables (e.g. postcode) correlate with it and produce unequal outcomes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Amazon's experimental hiring tool shows historical bias.
items.answer: Amazon built a machine-learning tool to rate CVs, trained on ten years of applications that came mostly from men; it penalised CVs containing "women's" and was abandoned (reported 2018). The model learned past hiring patterns in a male-dominated industry and reproduced them, showing how historical inequality enters algorithms.
items.markingKey: Context (Amazon built a machine-learning tool to rate CVs, trained on ten years of applications that came mostly from men; it penalised CVs containing "women's" and was abandoned (reported 2018).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A model whose decision process humans can follow directly, such as a decision tree or a simple scoring rule"?
items.answer: interpretable model
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of interpretable model.

items.stem: "If an algorithm is accurate, it does not need to be explainable." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: People affected by decisions have a right to understand and contest them, and explanations help find hidden bias; accuracy on average does not justify a particular decision.
items.markingKey: People affected by decisions have a right to understand and contest them, and explanations help find hidden bias; accuracy on average does not justify a particular decision. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a black-box model and an interpretable model.
items.answer: An interpretable model's logic can be followed by humans (e.g. a points-based score); a black-box model's internal workings are hidden or too complex to understand, so only inputs and outputs are observable.
items.markingKey: An interpretable model's logic can be followed by humans (e.g. a points-based score); a black-box model's internal workings are hidden or too complex to understand, so only inputs and outputs are observable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the DSA recommender-transparency rules shows regulation for transparency.
items.answer: From 2023–24 very large platforms in the EU must explain the main parameters of their recommender systems and offer a feed not based on profiling (e.g. TikTok and Instagram added chronological or non-personalised feeds in the EU). Requiring explanations and alternatives gives users some insight and choice, without forcing companies to publish code.
items.markingKey: Context (From 2023–24 very large platforms in the EU must explain the main parameters of their recommender systems and offer a feed not based on profiling (e.g. TikTok and Instagram added chronological or non-personalised feeds in the EU).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: requiring explanations and alternatives gives users some insight and choice, without forcing companies to publish code. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to regulation for transparency.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The data subject shall have the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision."
— GDPR, Article 22(3)

Explain how the right in the source relates to explainability.
items.answer: Contesting a decision is only meaningful if the person understands the reasons for it, so the right implies some explanation of the logic involved and human review.
items.markingKey: Contesting a decision is only meaningful if the person understands the reasons for it, so the right implies some explanation of the logic involved and human review. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A bank uses a complex machine-learning model to decide loan applications. Evaluate whether it should switch to a simpler, interpretable model.
items.answer: Accuracy vs explainability trade-off; legal duties (GDPR Art 22, EU AI Act high-risk credit scoring); customer trust; possibility of explanation tools; recommendation with justification.
items.markingKey: Accuracy vs explainability trade-off; legal duties (GDPR Art 22, EU AI Act high-risk credit scoring); customer trust; possibility of explanation tools; recommendation with justification.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "explainability"?
options: A model whose decision process humans can follow directly, such as a decision tree or a simple scoring rule
Under the EU AI Act, an AI system used in areas such as hiring, credit scoring, education or law enforcement that must meet strict requirements
When biased outputs influence future data, reinforcing the bias, as in predictive policing
The ability to give understandable reasons for a particular output of an algorithm
items.answer: The ability to give understandable reasons for a particular output of an algorithm
items.markingKey: D. "explainability" is the ability to give understandable reasons for a particular output of an algorithm.

items.stem: Explain why the "black box" problem makes it hard to challenge algorithmic decisions.
items.answer: If neither the affected person nor the organisation can see why the system produced an output, the person cannot identify errors or bias, and the organisation cannot justify the decision, so appeals and accountability are weakened.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If neither the affected person nor the organisation can see why the system produced an output, the person cannot identify errors or bias, and the organisation cannot justify the decision, so appeals and accountability are weakened. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which State v. Loomis (Wisconsin, 2016) shows the black box problem.
items.answer: Eric Loomis argued his sentence was influenced by a COMPAS score he could not examine because the algorithm was a trade secret; the court allowed its use but required warnings about its limitations. A proprietary algorithm influenced a liberty decision without the defendant being able to see or challenge its reasoning.
items.markingKey: Context (Eric Loomis argued his sentence was influenced by a COMPAS score he could not examine because the algorithm was a trade secret; the court allowed its use but required warnings about its limitations.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a proprietary algorithm influenced a liberty decision without the defendant being able to see or challenge its reasoning. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the black box problem.

items.stem: A student claims: "Publishing an algorithm's source code makes it fully transparent and accountable." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Code alone may be unintelligible to most people and does not show the training data, how it is used or its effects; meaningful transparency needs explanations, documentation and audits.
items.markingKey: Code alone may be unintelligible to most people and does not show the training data, how it is used or its effects; meaningful transparency needs explanations, documentation and audits. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Explainable AI solves the black box problem." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Explainability tools help but do not fully solve the problem; they need to be combined with audits, documentation and the right to contest.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tools such as LIME, SHAP and counterfactuals give insight into decisions; interpretable models can be used for high-stakes cases. Arguments against: explanations can be approximate or misleading; they may not reveal bias in training data; organisations still control what is disclosed. Supported judgement: Explainability tools help but do not fully solve the problem; they need to be combined with audits, documentation and the right to contest. items.stem: Which organisation, founded by Joy Buolamwini, campaigns for accountable AI?
items.answer: The Algorithmic Justice League
items.markingKey: The Algorithmic Justice League. Founded in 2016 after her research on facial analysis.

items.stem: Explain the difference between self-regulation by companies and legislation.
items.answer: Self-regulation relies on companies' own ethics principles and voluntary measures (e.g. AI ethics boards); legislation imposes binding duties with penalties, such as the EU AI Act or NYC Local Law 144.
items.markingKey: Self-regulation relies on companies' own ethics principles and voluntary measures (e.g. AI ethics boards); legislation imposes binding duties with penalties, such as the EU AI Act or NYC Local Law 144. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why accountability for algorithmic harms is difficult to assign.
items.answer: Many actors are involved – data providers, developers, vendors, the organisation using the system and officials who rely on it – and opaque systems make it hard to show where the error arose, so each can shift blame ("the computer did it").
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many actors are involved – data providers, developers, vendors, the organisation using the system and officials who rely on it – and opaque systems make it hard to show where the error arose, so each can shift blame ("the computer did it"). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the EU AI Act (2024) and explain what it reveals about regulation of algorithms.
items.answer: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, banning practices such as social scoring and setting strict obligations for high-risk systems, with fines of up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices. A binding, risk-based law gives regulators powers to require documentation, human oversight and conformity assessment before high-risk systems are used.
items.markingKey: Context (The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, banning practices such as social scoring and setting strict obligations for high-risk systems, with fines of up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a binding, risk-based law gives regulators powers to require documentation, human oversight and conformity assessment before high-risk systems are used. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to regulation of algorithms.

items.stem: A bias audit of an automated CV-screening tool, of the kind required by New York City Local Law 144, found that 158 of 400 female applicants and 144 of 350 male applicants were selected for interview. Calculate the selection rate for each group and the impact ratio (lower rate ÷ higher rate).
items.answer: 39.5% and 41.1%; impact ratio 0.96

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Algorithm audits make automated hiring fair."
items.answer: Audits improve visibility of bias but do not by themselves guarantee fairness without obligations to act and independent oversight.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measure disparities such as impact ratios; public summaries create pressure to improve. Arguments against: audits may only test limited groups and metrics; no obligation to change the tool (NYC LL144); auditors may be paid by the employer. Supported judgement: Audits improve visibility of bias but do not by themselves guarantee fairness without obligations to act and independent oversight.

items.stem: Define the term "right to contest".
items.answer: The right of a person affected by an automated decision to challenge it and obtain human review
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the right of a person affected by an automated decision to challenge it and obtain human review. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "The EU AI Act bans all use of AI in hiring." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It classifies AI used in recruitment as high-risk, which is allowed but must meet requirements such as risk management, data quality, documentation, human oversight and transparency.
items.markingKey: It classifies AI used in recruitment as high-risk, which is allowed but must meet requirements such as risk management, data quality, documentation, human oversight and transparency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We published our bias audit as required. Nobody told us what would happen if the ratios were poor."
— HR manager at a New York employer, interviewed for a 2024 study of Local Law 144

Explain one limitation of the law suggested by the source.
items.answer: The law requires audits and publication but does not require employers to fix poor results or set clear consequences, so transparency may not lead to change.
items.markingKey: The law requires audits and publication but does not require employers to fix poor results or set clear consequences, so transparency may not lead to change. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A bias audit of an automated CV-screening tool, of the kind required by New York City Local Law 144, found that 56 of 200 applicants with a disability and 68 of 150 applicants without a disability were selected for interview. Calculate the selection rate for each group and the impact ratio (lower rate ÷ higher rate).
items.answer: 28% and 45.3%; impact ratio 0.62

items.stem: In ProPublica's 2016 analysis of COMPAS in Broward County, Florida, what was the approximate false positive rate for Black defendants who did not reoffend, compared with white defendants?
items.answer: About 45% compared with about 23%
items.markingKey: A. Black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as likely to be labelled higher risk.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "transparency".
items.answer: Openness about how an algorithmic system works, what data it uses and how decisions are made
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: openness about how an algorithmic system works, what data it uses and how decisions are made. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which cities launched public AI/algorithm registers in 2020?
items.answer: Amsterdam and Helsinki
items.markingKey: D. Registers describe the purpose, data and oversight of city algorithms.

items.stem: Explain the difference between design bias and training data bias.
items.answer: Training data bias comes from unrepresentative or historically unequal data; design bias comes from choices made by developers, such as which variables to use, the goal to optimise or the definition of "success".
items.markingKey: Training data bias comes from unrepresentative or historically unequal data; design bias comes from choices made by developers, such as which variables to use, the goal to optimise or the definition of "success". items.stem: Explain the difference between transparency and explainability.
items.answer: Transparency is openness about a system in general (purpose, data, logic, who uses it); explainability is being able to give reasons for a specific output (why this person was refused).
items.markingKey: Transparency is openness about a system in general (purpose, data, logic, who uses it); explainability is being able to give reasons for a specific output (why this person was refused). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the EU AI Act uses a risk-based approach.
items.answer: AI systems differ greatly in potential harm; banning or heavily regulating all AI would block harmless uses, so obligations are matched to risk – strict rules for high-risk uses such as hiring or policing and light rules for low-risk uses.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: AI systems differ greatly in potential harm; banning or heavily regulating all AI would block harmless uses, so obligations are matched to risk – strict rules for high-risk uses such as hiring or policing and light rules for low-risk uses. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Black defendants were often predicted to be at a higher risk of recidivism than they actually were."
— ProPublica, "Machine Bias", May 2016

Explain what kind of error the source describes and why it matters.
items.answer: It describes false positives – people wrongly predicted to reoffend – which matter because they can lead to harsher bail or sentencing decisions for people who would not have reoffended.
items.markingKey: It describes false positives – people wrongly predicted to reoffend – which matter because they can lead to harsher bail or sentencing decisions for people who would not have reoffended. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"I could not cross-examine an algorithm."
— Paraphrase of the argument made on behalf of Eric Loomis, State v. Loomis, 2016

With reference to the source, explain why black-box algorithms raise concerns in justice systems.
items.answer: Defendants have a right to challenge evidence used against them; if a proprietary algorithm's reasoning is secret, they cannot test its accuracy or bias, undermining due process.
items.markingKey: Defendants have a right to challenge evidence used against them; if a proprietary algorithm's reasoning is secret, they cannot test its accuracy or bias, undermining due process. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Providers of high-risk AI systems shall ensure that their systems are designed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use."
— Summary of EU AI Act, Article 14 (human oversight), 2024

Explain how the requirement in the source contributes to accountability.
items.answer: Human oversight means a responsible person can monitor, understand and override the system, so decisions are not left solely to the machine and someone can be held answerable.
items.markingKey: Human oversight means a responsible person can monitor, understand and override the system, so decisions are not left solely to the machine and someone can be held answerable. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline one way in which COMPAS (USA) shows algorithmic bias in criminal justice.
items.answer: ProPublica's 2016 "Machine Bias" investigation of the COMPAS recidivism tool in Broward County found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as likely as white defendants to be labelled higher risk; Northpointe disputed the analysis. Unequal false positive rates meant the costs of errors fell disproportionately on Black defendants, influencing bail and sentencing decisions.
items.markingKey: Context (ProPublica's 2016 "Machine Bias" investigation of the COMPAS recidivism tool in Broward County found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as likely as white defendants to be labelled higher risk; Northpointe disputed the analysis.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: unequal false positive rates meant the costs of errors fell disproportionately on Black defendants, influencing bail and sentencing decisions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to algorithmic bias in criminal justice.

items.stem: Briefly describe Apple Card credit limits (2019) and explain what it reveals about the need for explainability.
items.answer: Some customers, including tech entrepreneur David Heinemeier Hansson, complained that women received much lower credit limits than their husbands; Goldman Sachs could not easily explain individual decisions. New York regulators later found no unlawful discrimination but criticised customer communication. Even without proven discrimination, the inability to explain decisions damaged trust and triggered an investigation.
items.markingKey: Context (Some customers, including tech entrepreneur David Heinemeier Hansson, complained that women received much lower credit limits than their husbands; Goldman Sachs could not easily explain individual decisions. New York regulators later found no unlawful discrimination but criticised customer communication.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: even without proven discrimination, the inability to explain decisions damaged trust and triggered an investigation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the need for explainability.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Dutch childcare-benefits scandal and explain what it reveals about accountability after algorithmic harm.
items.answer: After investigations showed a risk-scoring system and harsh enforcement wrongly accused thousands of families of fraud, the Dutch government resigned in 2021 and set up a compensation scheme; the data-protection authority fined the tax authority €2.75 million. Political, legal and financial accountability followed, but only after years of harm, showing the need for earlier oversight.
items.markingKey: Context (After investigations showed a risk-scoring system and harsh enforcement wrongly accused thousands of families of fraud, the Dutch government resigned in 2021 and set up a compensation scheme; the data-protection authority fined the tax authority €2.75 million.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: political, legal and financial accountability followed, but only after years of harm, showing the need for earlier oversight. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to accountability after algorithmic harm.

items.stem: An audit of a CV-screening model that rejects "unsuitable" applicants looked only at people who were later judged suitable for the job. Of 200 such women, 81 were wrongly flagged; of 200 such men, 36 were wrongly flagged. Calculate the false positive rate for each group and how many times higher one rate is than the other.
items.answer: women: 40.5%; men: 18%; 2.2 times higher for women

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Companies should be required to explain every decision made by their algorithms."
items.answer: Explanation should be mandatory and meaningful for high-stakes decisions (credit, jobs, justice), while low-stakes systems need general transparency.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people affected have a right to understand and contest decisions; explanations reveal bias and errors. Arguments against: some models cannot give simple explanations; trade secrets and gaming risks; low-stakes decisions (song recommendations) may not need explanation. Supported judgement: Explanation should be mandatory and meaningful for high-stakes decisions (credit, jobs, justice), while low-stakes systems need general transparency.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of one law or policy designed to make algorithms accountable.
items.answer: E.g. EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144, GDPR Art 22, Amsterdam/Helsinki registers; describe requirements; evaluate scope, enforcement, impact on stakeholders, loopholes; judgement.
items.markingKey: E.g. EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144, GDPR Art 22, Amsterdam/Helsinki registers; describe requirements; evaluate scope, enforcement, impact on stakeholders, loopholes; judgement.

items.stem: "Algorithms should not be used in criminal-justice decisions." Discuss.
items.answer: Given the stakes, algorithms should at most advise, be transparent and independently audited; fully automated decisions are not justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: documented bias (COMPAS); opacity and inability to challenge proprietary scores; liberty is at stake. Arguments against: human judges are also biased and inconsistent; transparent, audited tools could reduce disparities; tools may help prioritise resources. Supported judgement: Given the stakes, algorithms should at most advise, be transparent and independently audited; fully automated decisions are not justified. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that explainable AI solves the black box problem.
items.answer: Explainability tools help but do not fully solve the problem; they need to be combined with audits, documentation and the right to contest.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tools such as LIME, SHAP and counterfactuals give insight into decisions; interpretable models can be used for high-stakes cases. Arguments against: explanations can be approximate or misleading; they may not reveal bias in training data; organisations still control what is disclosed. Supported judgement: Explainability tools help but do not fully solve the problem; they need to be combined with audits, documentation and the right to contest. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When biased outputs influence future data, reinforcing the bias, as in predictive policing"?
items.answer: feedback loop (bias)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of feedback loop (bias).

items.stem: In State v. Loomis (2016), which court upheld the use of COMPAS scores in sentencing while warning about their limitations?
items.answer: The Wisconsin Supreme Court
items.markingKey: B. Loomis argued he could not challenge the proprietary algorithm.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The EU regulation (in force from August 2024) that classifies AI systems by risk – unacceptable, high, limited and minimal – with obligations for each level"?
items.answer: EU AI Act
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of EU AI Act.

items.stem: A student claims: "Algorithms are objective because they are based on mathematics." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mathematics processes the data and goals chosen by people; biased data and design choices produce biased outputs, as COMPAS and Amazon's CV tool showed.
items.markingKey: Mathematics processes the data and goals chosen by people; biased data and design choices produce biased outputs, as COMPAS and Amazon's CV tool showed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why full transparency about an algorithm is not always desirable.
items.answer: Publishing exact rules could let people game the system (spammers, fraudsters), expose trade secrets and personal data in training sets; meaningful explanation and independent audits may be better than publishing code.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Publishing exact rules could let people game the system (spammers, fraudsters), expose trade secrets and personal data in training sets; meaningful explanation and independent audits may be better than publishing code. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between legislation and self-regulation by companies.
items.answer: Self-regulation relies on companies' own ethics principles and voluntary measures (e.g. AI ethics boards); legislation imposes binding duties with penalties, such as the EU AI Act or NYC Local Law 144.
items.markingKey: Self-regulation relies on companies' own ethics principles and voluntary measures (e.g. AI ethics boards); legislation imposes binding duties with penalties, such as the EU AI Act or NYC Local Law 144. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): An algorithm can discriminate by race even if race is not one of its inputs.
Reason (R): Variables such as postcode can act as proxies for race.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Proxies carry protected information indirectly.

items.stem: Briefly explain why there can be a trade-off between accuracy and explainability.
items.answer: Complex models (deep neural networks) can find subtle patterns and be more accurate, but their millions of parameters make individual decisions hard to explain, while simpler, interpretable models may be less accurate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Complex models (deep neural networks) can find subtle patterns and be more accurate, but their millions of parameters make individual decisions hard to explain, while simpler, interpretable models may be less accurate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why independent audits are important for algorithmic accountability.
items.answer: Organisations have incentives to present their systems positively; independent auditors can test outcomes across groups, check data and legality, and publish findings, giving external evidence on which regulators and the public can act.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Organisations have incentives to present their systems positively; independent auditors can test outcomes across groups, check data and legality, and publish findings, giving external evidence on which regulators and the public can act. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Gender Shades (2018) as an example, explain bias from unrepresentative training data.
items.answer: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial facial-analysis systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ and found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women but 0.8% for lighter-skinned men. Systems trained mostly on lighter-skinned, male faces performed worst on under-represented groups; the companies later improved their systems.
items.markingKey: Context (Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial facial-analysis systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ and found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women but 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: systems trained mostly on lighter-skinned, male faces performed worst on under-represented groups; the companies later improved their systems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bias from unrepresentative training data.

items.stem: Using Apple Card credit limits (2019) as an example, explain the need for explainability.
items.answer: Some customers, including tech entrepreneur David Heinemeier Hansson, complained that women received much lower credit limits than their husbands; Goldman Sachs could not easily explain individual decisions. New York regulators later found no unlawful discrimination but criticised customer communication. Even without proven discrimination, the inability to explain decisions damaged trust and triggered an investigation.
items.markingKey: Context (Some customers, including tech entrepreneur David Heinemeier Hansson, complained that women received much lower credit limits than their husbands; Goldman Sachs could not easily explain individual decisions. New York regulators later found no unlawful discrimination but criticised customer communication.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: even without proven discrimination, the inability to explain decisions damaged trust and triggered an investigation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the need for explainability.

items.stem: A bias audit of an automated CV-screening tool, of the kind required by New York City Local Law 144, found that 73 of 400 applicants over 50 and 61 of 150 applicants under 50 were selected for interview. Calculate the selection rate for each group and the impact ratio (lower rate ÷ higher rate).
items.answer: 18.2% and 40.7%; impact ratio 0.45

items.stem: An audit of a CV-screening model that rejects "unsuitable" applicants looked only at people who were later judged suitable for the job. Of 300 such people in group A, 118 were wrongly flagged; of 200 such people in group B, 43 were wrongly flagged. Calculate the false positive rate for each group and how many times higher one rate is than the other.
items.answer: people in group A: 39.3%; people in group B: 21.5%; 1.8 times higher for people in group A

items.stem: Tariq writes: "If an algorithm is accurate, it does not need to be explainable." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: People affected by decisions have a right to understand and contest them, and explanations help find hidden bias; accuracy on average does not justify a particular decision.
items.markingKey: People affected by decisions have a right to understand and contest them, and explanations help find hidden bias; accuracy on average does not justify a particular decision. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Dutch childcare-benefits scandal as an example, explain accountability after algorithmic harm.
items.answer: After investigations showed a risk-scoring system and harsh enforcement wrongly accused thousands of families of fraud, the Dutch government resigned in 2021 and set up a compensation scheme; the data-protection authority fined the tax authority €2.75 million. Political, legal and financial accountability followed, but only after years of harm, showing the need for earlier oversight.
items.markingKey: Context (After investigations showed a risk-scoring system and harsh enforcement wrongly accused thousands of families of fraud, the Dutch government resigned in 2021 and set up a compensation scheme; the data-protection authority fined the tax authority €2.75 million.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: political, legal and financial accountability followed, but only after years of harm, showing the need for earlier oversight. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to accountability after algorithmic harm.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Companies should be required to explain every decision made by their algorithms."
items.answer: Explanation should be mandatory and meaningful for high-stakes decisions (credit, jobs, justice), while low-stakes systems need general transparency.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people affected have a right to understand and contest decisions; explanations reveal bias and errors. Arguments against: some models cannot give simple explanations; trade secrets and gaming risks; low-stakes decisions (song recommendations) may not need explanation. Supported judgement: Explanation should be mandatory and meaningful for high-stakes decisions (credit, jobs, justice), while low-stakes systems need general transparency.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that legislation is the most effective way to make algorithms accountable.
items.answer: Legislation is essential to make accountability enforceable, but it works best alongside independent audits, investigative journalism and public registers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binding duties and penalties (EU AI Act fines up to 7%); creates enforceable rights for affected people. Arguments against: laws lag behind technology; enforcement capacity is limited; audits, journalism (ProPublica) and civil society often reveal harms first. Supported judgement: Legislation is essential to make accountability enforceable, but it works best alongside independent audits, investigative journalism and public registers.
